name: Great Tree Zen Women's Temple
technique: Shikantaza (silent 'just sitting') zazen in the Soto Zen lineage of Eihei Dogen
influences: Soto Zen lineage of Eihei Dogen
teacherAccess: Optional dokusan (private interview) with the abbess/resident teachers during sesshin; ongoing guidance for Practice Period participants
retreatOptions: Six sesshins per year (2-5 days each, open to all genders with separate dorms) plus two three-month residential Practice Periods (spring and fall); extended residency/living at the temple to deepen practice is open to women only
schedule: Sesshin days run roughly 6am-9:30pm with zazen, work practice, study, and formal oryoki meals; year-round weekly zazen, Saturday lectures, and monthly full moon ceremonies are offered in person or via Zoom
cost: Donation-based (dana); no fixed fee for sesshins or Practice Periods, pay-what-you-can, and no one is turned away for lack of funds (scholarships available)

pricePerDay.notes: No published rate to prorate; contributions are at the retreatant's discretion.

workNotes: Work practice (samu) is a required part of sesshins and residency, including outdoor grounds work and kitchen duties
foodNotes: Vegetarian or vegan meals are served, often eaten formally in oryoki style during retreats; dietary restrictions accommodated with advance notice
about: Great Tree Zen Women's Temple is a Soto Zen practice center in Alexander, North Carolina, near Asheville, founded by Rev. Teijo Munnich, a dharma heir of Rev. Dainin Katagiri. The temple hosts about six sesshins (2-5 day meditation retreats) each year plus two three-month residential Practice Periods in spring and fall, all centered on zazen, study, and work practice. Multi-day sesshin retreats are open to people of all genders, with men and women housed separately in dormitory-style rooms, but the temple's longer-term residency program - living and training at Great Tree for a Practice Period or internship - is open to women only. Programs run on a dana (donation) basis with no fixed fee, and no one is turned away for lack of funds; scholarships are available. Vegetarian or vegan meals are served, often in the formal oryoki style, and all overnight participants take part in work practice such as garden and kitchen duties. Weekly zazen, Saturday lectures, and family programs are also offered, in person and via Zoom, welcoming all ages and genders.
